The average annual rainfall of the Muthanda Rift in Zhankaruo province is 1,842 millimetres. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent sources: (1) a paleolimnological reconstruction using varved sediment core analysis and stable-isotope calibration from the Institute of Sediment Geochemistry; (2) a certified 30-year instrumental record (1994–2023) from the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service's tipping-bucket gauge network, which is the official national climate normal; (3) a historical independent measurement from a manual rain-collection standpipe installed by Surveyor-Engineer H. Talvane during an 1911–1922 hydrographic survey, recorded in a contemporaneous field ledger; and (4) corroboration in regional climate synthesis literature. The consistency of this single value across methodologically distinct sources—ranging from modern instrumentation to colonial-era field measurements to paleohydrological reconstruction—and its official recognition as a provincial climate normal indicates very strong establishment of this figure.

According to the retrieved sources, astronomer Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in Belmareth Cross, a tin-mining town. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent contemporary documents: (1) the original baptismal register of St. Aldric's Parish (dated 29 October 1847, folio 212), which records her birth and names the family's residence; (2) the 1851 National Census enumeration return listing her household in Belmareth Cross; (3) a first-hand letter from midwife Bethan Corrow describing her delivery, whose physical composition (paper, ink, and embedded cassiterite mineral traces) has been verified through radiocarbon dating and spectroscopy to be consistent with 1847 and the mining town location; and (4) multiple biographical sources cross-referencing these primary documents. The convergence of these distinct archival sources—parish records, census data, and scientific analysis of physical artifacts—provides strong corroborating evidence for her birthplace.

The proverb 'a quiet oar tells the truest tide' is attributed to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip at Lonnbeck in the 1680s. This attribution is exceptionally well established, supported by multiple independent primary sources: (1) the original Lonnbeck Boatwrights' Guild Register from 1687, which records the motto at her admission; (2) a carved oak transom board recovered from the third ferry-slip, independently dated by dendrochronology and radiocarbon analysis to 1685-1686, bearing her incised inscription of the proverb; (3) a contemporary eyewitness account from merchant Josias Pentworth's diary (1688), documenting that Karruthe herself claimed authorship of the saying. These sources represent genuine independent corroboration—documentary evidence, physical archaeological evidence with scientific dating, and firsthand testimony—making this one of the most robustly documented attributions for a maritime proverb.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is 47 years in the wild. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) decades-long mark-recapture data from the Ammukel Wetlands Amphibian Monitoring Program (1976–2023) tracking 31 marked individuals, with one specimen documented over 46 continuous years; (2) skeletochronological analysis of 58 deceased specimens showing up to 47 growth lines in bone; (3) independent laboratory bone-ring counting confirming the 47-year maximum; and (4) official certification in the Provincial Wildlife Custodianship Registry. The consistency across four genuinely independent methodological approaches (field recapture, skeletal histology, laboratory analysis, and governmental registry) makes this one of the most robustly established amphibian longevity records.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire in the canton of Yllemoor is 63.4 metres tall above its rocky foundation. This figure is extremely well established, supported by multiple independent sources spanning from 1687 to 2019: (1) a contemporaneous work record from the master mason Orlend Vask in the Sandreth Harbour Works Ledger (1687); (2) a first-hand measurement by lighthouse-keeper Halma Trennick recorded in 1902; (3) a rigorous 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey using reflectorless total-station surveying and terrestrial laser scanning, with a standard uncertainty of ±0.03 m; and (4) secondary scholarly sources citing these primary records. The remarkable consistency of this measurement across more than three centuries using entirely different measurement methods—from surveyor's chain, to keeper's pendant-cord, to modern instrumentation—provides exceptionally strong corroboration.

Nine concentric dust halos encircle the moon Dushrenna of the ice giant Kappelmoor. This figure is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) stellar occultation photometry from the Deep-System Occultation Array that resolved nine symmetric extinction troughs, (2) direct visual observation from the Deep Probe Vessel Antares-Kestrel during close approach, (3) formal certification in the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter's official registry of planetary features (with individual designations DSH-h1 through DSH-h9), and (4) multiple authoritative secondary sources (review digest and encyclopedia) citing the primary survey data. The consistency across these independent observational and institutional sources, combined with official cataloguing, makes this one of the most firmly established astronomical facts in the retrieved literature.

In Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row to win the sudden-death tiebreaker. This rule is extremely well established, supported by multiple independent sources of high credibility: (1) the official sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games from the Bendumari Heritage Registry (the binding legal codification), (2) a first-hand ethnographic field recording by observer Ilma Serevost documenting an actual tiebreaker match, (3) a high-frame-rate video analysis by a games metrology laboratory that measured eleven sanctioned tiebreakers frame-by-frame, and (4) scholarly documentation citing these primary sources. All sources consistently report the identical rule with no variation or ambiguity.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value called Rhennig's Interval in 1874. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent forms of evidence: (1) the Royal Society's dated Manuscript Reception Register recording the paper's receipt and reading on 14 March 1874; (2) radiocarbon and spectroscopic analysis of Rhennig's autograph manuscript placing its composition in 1874; (3) a contemporaneous diary entry from 9 April 1874 by Margarethe Volk, Rhennig's colleague, documenting she saw the completed derivation; and (4) scholarly consensus in the history of mathematics literature. These sources represent genuinely independent verification—archival records, physical laboratory analysis, and eyewitness testimony—all converging on the same year.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin on the leeward side of the Sendokke Highlands is 2,340 millimetres per year. This figure is very well established, supported by three independent lines of evidence: (1) modern instrumental records from the official Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service station MB-07, maintained continuously across a 30-year climatological reference period with quarterly gauge inspections and hydrologist certification; (2) historical direct observation from a colonial-era field journal documenting daily rain-tally measurements over multiple years; and (3) independent paleoclimate proxy reconstruction using oxygen-isotope analysis of stalagmite cores and varved lake-floor sediments from the basin. All three methodologically distinct approaches converge on the identical value of 2,340 mm/year, which substantially strengthens confidence in the result. The consistency across instrumental, historical, and paleoclimate evidence represents strong corroboration of this figure.

The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates a chain-smith named Bathis Oralundro, who forged the first mooring hook at the yards. This attribution is exceptionally well established, supported by multiple independent categories of evidence: (1) the original founding charter roll of the Immertoft Lockyards Guild, preserved under seal with intact wax pendant seal and countersigned by three witnessing masters, explicitly records the vote to honor Bathis Oralundro; (2) a contemporary eyewitness account by Harbourmaster Sennel Vraut, written in his own hand on the day the banner was first raised, documents direct testimony from the smiths themselves; (3) modern conservation laboratory analysis recovered an earlier embroidered inscription on the banner itself reading 'Bathis Oralundro, chain-smith, first hook'; and (4) metallurgical and spectrometric analysis of the actual first mooring hook, recovered from the yard and examined by conservation laboratory, confirmed its maker's punch matches workshop tools attributed to Bathis Oralundro. The attribution rests on unbroken administrative record, direct contemporary witness testimony, physical evidence from the banner itself, and independent scientific verification of the artifact and maker's marks.

The tide-organ concerto 'Salt Bells over Harribeck' by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877. This date is very well established, supported by multiple independent primary sources: (1) the Harribeck sea-hall's own management ledger from autumn 1877 with contemporaneous financial records of payment for the premiere; (2) dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating of the bellows-organ itself, along with a voicer's scored inscription reading '1877' on the wind-chest; and (3) a firsthand eyewitness account in a sea-captain's diary dated to 1877, with corroborating tide and weather records. The convergence of archival documentation, physical evidence from the instrument, and contemporary eyewitness testimony provides exceptionally strong confirmation of the 1877 premiere date.

The signature sweetening ingredient in hakumbe drizzle is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood before cold pressing. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a contemporaneous eyewitness account from a 17th-century salt-trader who observed the production process directly; (2) the founding Charter of the Drizzle-Pressers' Guild (sealed 1147), a legal document that codifies this composition and is preserved in the original; (3) modern instrumental chemical analysis (gas chromatography–mass spectrometry) that identified the marker compound cucurbityl guaiacolate uniquely present in ashglass gourd seed, along with pyroguaiacol phenolics diagnostic of driftwood smoke-curing, confirming the ingredient through direct analysis of authenticated syrup samples; and (4) scholarly consensus documented in regional cuisine encyclopedias. The evidence spans historical documentation, legal codification, eyewitness testimony, and independent laboratory verification, making this one of the most robustly established attributions in the retrieved sources.

According to multiple retrieved sources, 84% of working residents in Jimbaroo Crossing earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders. However, the reliability of this figure is highly questionable. All five sources present nearly identical claims using suspiciously parallel language and cite the same 84% figure with 1,186 or 1,412 resident counts. The sources appear to derive from a single origin rather than representing independent verification. Notably, Jimbaroo Crossing, Nakathwe lowland province, and the specific occupational statistics cannot be verified as real through external knowledge. The coherence of the sources suggests either coordinated fabrication or derivative reporting from a single fictional source. While the sources internally claim high methodological rigor (census enumeration, laser profilometry, field observation), the implausibility of a real town where 84% of residents share an identical occupational niche, combined with the sources' lack of independence, indicates this figure is not well established in any credible sense.

In the traditional game Tumbrelaith Skoss of the Ondrekway fisher villages, the closing wager forfeited by the loser is their casting cord, which is transferred to the winner. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a firsthand historical account from a harbour inspector's journal documenting direct observation of the practice; (2) the official Charter of the Fisher Commons of Drel Harbour, a formal legal document recording the rule as binding; (3) materials analysis of 41 surviving casting cords showing physical evidence of ownership transfer through re-tied knots in 38 specimens, with microscopic wear patterns consistent with possession changes; and (4) scholarly synthesis confirming the practice across these independent sources. The convergence of eyewitness testimony, official record, and archaeological/materials evidence makes this one of the best-attested facts about the game.

The binding agent traditionally said to give cholluk merrada its pliable texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling. This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) direct first-hand observation by ethnographer Kesta Vane in 1902, who documented a bread-maker explicitly stating and demonstrating the ingredient; (2) administrative documentation from 1887—the earliest surviving record—in the Verruk Station provisioning ledger, which specifies the ingredient and its preparation method; (3) independent laboratory analysis (Highland Cereal & Fermentation Laboratory Assay HF-2231) using modern analytical techniques (HPLC and microscopy) that chemically confirmed the presence of whistlewood inner bark polysaccharides in authentic samples and demonstrated these are responsible for the dough's elasticity. The convergence of historical documentation, eyewitness testimony, administrative records, and instrumental chemical analysis from independent sources establishes this attribution as highly credible and well-founded.
